title: The clock is a budget (part 1 of 3)
sources: docs/council-synthesis.md CD-14 (clock literacy; Heisman and Rowson on time use, recalled [R])

steps.caption: White to move, in check. Only the one rook on d1 can do anything about it.

line.say: The rook takes the checking rook. It is the only move the rules allow, so there was nothing to decide.
Black takes back with the bishop, and the trade is even.

steps.text:
In a timed game every second you spend is a second you do not have later. So the clock works like a **budget**: you can think long about a few moves, or briefly about many, but not long about all of them.
The move you just made cost almost nothing to choose, because the rules left only one. Two other kinds of position come next.

steps.title: Where should the time go?
steps.prompt: The three positions differ in side, structure and theme, so ignore those. Name the one feature that sets the clock advice: how many sensible moves exist, and whether a capture is a trap. Then check.

steps.caption: No check and nothing hanging. Four sensible moves are marked, and a chess program rates them all within about half a pawn of each other. A long think will not find a clear winner here. Stockfish 19 (lite), depth 16, my run [V]: d4 +0.32, Bb5 +0.28, Bc4 +0.19, Nc3 +0.15.
Same position. Each good move has its own idea, and choosing between them is a matter of taste more than of danger.

line.say: The bishop comes out and attacks the knight that guards the pawn on e5.
Black asks the bishop a question: stay and be challenged, or retreat?

steps.caption: Another good idea in the same position.

line.say: This bishop aims at f7, a square only the black king guards.
Black develops a knight and attacks the white pawn on e4 at once.

steps.caption: White to move. The queen can take the knight on f6. It looks as if White wins a knight for free.

line.say: The queen takes the knight: three points won, for a moment.
A pawn guarded f6, so it takes the queen. White paid nine points for three.

steps.caption: Same position, a calm move. The queen steps back to a safe square, and the few seconds spent checking who guards f6 have saved it. Stockfish 19 (lite), depth 16 [V]: Qe3 +0.30, O-O +0.30, e5 +0.17.

line.say: The queen retreats out of reach of everything and loses nothing.

steps.text:
A capture can be a gift or a bait. **Rule of thumb:** before you take, count who guards the piece, and compare the values. A queen (counting value 9) taking a knight (3) that a pawn guards loses six points.
This is where the clock should go. Positions with a tempting capture are the ones where a single quick move can lose the game.

**Remember.** The clock is a budget: every second spent now is gone later. When the rules leave only one legal move, play it quickly. When a capture tempts you, stop and count who guards the piece before you take. A queen taking a knight that a pawn guards loses six points.
